item.title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
item.description: By Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, Rujun Han (Washington University in St. Louis; Google Cloud AI Research; Google Cloud; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill) EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning, by Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, and Rujun Han, with fourteen more authors including Burak Gokturk, Tomas Pfister, and Chen-Yu Lee. Huang did this work while interning at Google Cloud AI Research, and the affiliation list covers Washington University in St. Louis, Google Cloud AI Research, Google Cloud, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Here is the premise, and it is a reasonable one. As language models become agents, the scarce resource for training shifts from curated text data to interactive environments. Those environments are hand-built: someone hardcodes interaction logic and a verifier, and the result behaves identically whether it faces a novice or a competent policy. Two failure modes follow. A static environment cannot target the specific weaknesses of the policy you actually have, and once the policy learns to solve its existing tasks, the environment has nothing left to teach. Automated environment generation exists as an alternative, with systems like GenEnv simulating environments and their feedback inside a model, VeriEnv synthesizing executable environments programmatically, and SWE-smith generating new task instances within an existing benchmark. But those pipelines are domain-specific, each built separately for web navigation, programming, or tool use, and because both tasks and verifiers come out of a model, teams over-generate and filter heavily without ever guaranteeing correctness. EnvHarness takes a different position: stop authoring new environments, and reshape the ones you already trust.

item.title: FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis
item.description: By Kou Shi, Zun Wang, Qisheng Su (MoE Key Lab of BIPC, University of Science and Technology of China; Shanghai AI Laboratory; Fudan University) FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis, by Kou Shi, Zun Wang, and Qisheng Su, with ten more authors including Feng Zhao as corresponding author. The affiliations are the MoE Key Lab of BIPC at the University of Science and Technology of China, Shanghai AI Laboratory, and Fudan University. The problem this paper attacks is concrete: training terminal agents needs scalable, executable supervision, and every synthesized terminal task is a tightly coupled bundle of an instruction, an initialized environment, a reference solution, and an executable verifier, packaged in the Harbor format that Terminal-Bench uses. If those artifacts are generated under inconsistent assumptions you get tasks that cannot be solved or that grade incorrectly. Two failure mechanisms dominate multi-stage synthesis pipelines. First, information loss: source material rich in capabilities, dependencies, intermediate states, input-output contracts, and procedural constraints gets progressively compressed into a simplified task description, preserving only a fraction of the available structure. Second, artifact drift: an instruction references a file never realized in the environment, a solution assumes a different schema or dependency version, or a verifier tests a state the generated task cannot produce. Passing textual specifications between generation stages mitigates neither problem, because text is not a shared realized state.

item.title: SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?
item.description: By Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, Yining Zheng (Shanghai Innovation Institute; Fudan University) SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?, by Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, and Yining Zheng, with Yuxin Wang and Xipeng Qiu as corresponding authors, all affiliated with the Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University. The motivation is worth stating carefully because this is not benchmark inflation. Software now functions as part of the scientific instrument itself: simulations, instrument processing pipelines, surrogate models, candidate search in chemistry and biology, reproduction of published results. A defective patch to that software corrupts not just a program but the evidence behind a scientific conclusion. Existing coding-agent evaluations mostly report aggregate task success, which cannot tell you why an agent failed on scientific code. This paper contributes a repository-level benchmark of 119 tasks drawn from 98 unique GitHub repositories across 20 scientific domains, plus a failure-mode taxonomy and a paired ablation on scientific knowledge. Code and data are public through GitHub and Hugging Face under the OpenMOSS organization, with a leaderboard maintained separately. Scale first. Input repositories average about 80,600 non-empty lines, ranging from 174 to over two million. Reference patches add an average of 117.81 lines and delete 44.53. Chemistry is the largest domain at 24 tasks, then materials science with 16, biology with 13, biomedical engineering with 12, physics with 11; six domains contribute a single task each. Tasks fall into three paradigms: Issue-driven at 52 tasks, repairing known historical defects under low distortion; Expert-exploratory at 49, where the agent must autonomously find an unknown root cause from an observed anomaly such as abnormal convergence or biased results, with any underlying issue used only as

item.title: Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation
item.description: By Silin Chen, Haoyi Teng, Xiaodong Gu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Chongqing University) Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation, by Silin Chen and Haoyi Teng as equal first authors, Xiaodong Gu as corresponding author, with Yuling Shi, Jiale Huang, Yongpan Wang, Hongyu Zhang, and Haibing Guan. The affiliations are Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chongqing University. The setting is zero-to-all code generation: an agent receives natural-language requirements and must construct an entire software project from nothing while maintaining a modular repository architecture throughout. Most existing systems quietly assume the opposite, that component boundaries, package organization, and dependency graphs are already given, which is why repository-completion work looks so much better than it should. The authors' diagnosis of prior systems, including RPG, the strongest graph-based baseline, is that they treat software design as a static artifact: a perfect architectural blueprint generated in one initial planning stage, then rigidly executed. Anyone who has shipped software knows the blueprint is wrong by the time implementation starts; generated code reveals whether planned components were ever cohesive or whether dependency edges are entangled. Repo0's answer is continuous structural evolution around an explicit architectural state, instantiated as what they call a Dual-DAG. Two directed acyclic graphs plus an alignment relation. The requirement-level DAG holds high-level requirements decomposed into sub-requirements, and its edges encode functional coordination: two requirements logically used together and needing joint consideration for behavior, inputs, and outputs. item.title: FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
item.description: By Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, Zhiying Wu (MAIS and NLPR, CASIA; UCAS; WeChat, Tencent) FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving, by Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, and Zhiying Wu, with Bingning Wang as project leader and Ran He. The affiliations are the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences through its MAIS and NLPR labs, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and WeChat at Tencent; the first author completed the work during an internship at WeChat. Context for the audience: attention cost during prefill grows with the square of sequence length, and every training-free sparse-attention method lives or dies on three practical questions. Does accuracy survive aggressive sparsity? Is the kernel competitive with current dense implementations rather than last generation's? And does it work inside a real serving stack with paged KV cache and continuous batching? Their previous FlashPrefill answered none of those fully. It discovered patterns instantaneously using mean-pooled keys and max-based dynamic thresholding, avoiding the global sorting that Top-k selection requires, but accuracy degraded without bound under extreme sparsity, the kernel was built on FlashAttention-2's execution model, which leaves Hopper tensor-core throughput on the table, and it assumed a contiguous KV layout incompatible with any modern serving framework. V2 addresses exactly these three gaps.

item.title: FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills
item.description: By Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, Ran Li (Southeast University; Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills, by Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, and Ran Li, with Yishu Wang, Shengxiang Xu, Hanmo Liu, Shaowu Pan, and Shimin Di. The affiliations are Southeast University, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The gap this paper identifies is real and worth articulating precisely. Workflow-based agents construct procedures at inference time: decomposition, tool calls, code generation, checking, repair. But whatever structure a successful episode discovers gets discarded when the episode ends. Skill libraries preserve reusable routines as executable objects, yet they are typically assembled offline for a fixed task distribution rather than growing from the agent's own problem solving. Text memories such as Agent Workflow Memory sit in between: they describe what worked but cannot be invoked or validated, so reuse still depends on the model re-deriving the procedure from prose. FlowEvo is a training-free framework that closes this loop: successful workflows are compiled into callable skill records stored in a persistent bank, and those skills feed back into later workflow construction either through direct execution or as structured context. Model weights never change.

item.title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't
item.description: By Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, Hanwen Xing (Princeton University; UC San Diego; Stanford University; University of Southern California; Johns Hopkins University) Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't. First authors Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, and Hanwen Xing, working across Princeton University, UC San Diego, Stanford University, the University of Southern California, and Johns Hopkins University. The paper asks a question most skill evaluations skip entirely: when do agent skills actually help, why do they work, and where do they fail. If you maintain SKILL.md-style packages in production agents, this is a measurement paper worth your attention. Here is the gap being addressed. Skills are structured knowledge packages injected into an agent's environment at inference time. Existing evaluations report aggregate task success with and without skills, which tells you nothing about mechanism. A skill could win because it injects missing facts, because it stabilizes execution, or by accident. Those three explanations imply very different engineering investments, and aggregate success rates cannot distinguish them. The study design is the strongest part of the paper. The authors compare three conditions built from identical source material: Raw, meaning no prior experience; Workflow Memory, meaning cleaned execution traces from prior runs handed to the agent directly; and Skill, meaning a standardized SKILL.md document distilled from exactly the same traces. Because Workflow Memory and Skill are constructed from the same underlying trajectories, any difference between them isolates the effect of representation rather than the effect of having seen past experience. item.title: FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution
item.description: By Shuo Yang, Xiaoze Fan, Melissa Pan (UC Berkeley; University of Texas at Austin; MIT; University of Michigan) FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution. Shuo Yang, Xiaoze Fan, and Melissa Pan led the work, with the author group spanning UC Berkeley, the University of Texas at Austin, MIT, and the University of Michigan—the PDF's first page lists correspondence through Berkeley and UT Austin addresses. The claim: a serving stack co-designed for consumer hardware can run frontier-scale mixture-of-experts models interactively on machines people already own. Skeptical? So was I. The numbers are specific enough to check. The problem first. Open-weight frontier models like GLM-5.2 at 753 billion parameters and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284 billion parameters with 13 billion active per token are free to download and expensive to run. They assume datacenter GPUs whose clusters cost millions of dollars, and hosted APIs remain burdensome for individuals as agentic applications multiply inference demand. Meanwhile over one hundred million consumer machines have discrete GPUs—Steam alone reports more than 200 million monthly active users with discrete NVIDIA GPUs on roughly 72 percent of surveyed systems. Mixture-of-experts architectures make edge serving plausible because each token activates a small subset of experts—DeepSeek-V4-Flash routes to 6 of 256 experts in each of its 43 layers—but existing engines waste that sparsity in three distinct ways.

item.title: ASI-Bench: At the Dawn of Artificial Superintelligence
item.description: By Junwei Zhou, Zhen Sun, Binyu Li (Tsinghua University; University of Michigan; MIT; Harvard University) ASI-Bench: At the Dawn of Artificial Superintelligence. Core authors Junwei Zhou, Zhen Sun, and Binyu Li, from a large collaboration spanning Tsinghua University, the University of Michigan, MIT, Harvard University, Carnegie Mellon University, and several other institutions. The title oversells it; the benchmark does not. What this paper actually delivers is a controlled measurement of how fast frontier agents fall apart when you withdraw human methodological guidance, and that measurement is worth your time. The premise: today's AI mostly learns, compresses, and applies existing human knowledge. Benchmarks test whether systems produce correct answers from learned knowledge or complete tasks under heavy human specification. Nobody jointly measures innovative exploration—choosing how to attack an open research problem—and autonomous scientific execution across general domains, within one project, with guidance progressively removed. Existing options each cover a slice: Humanity's Last Exam is academic question answering; Terminal-Bench is terminal tasks; ScienceAgentBench is scientific analysis under largely fixed workflows; PaperBench is research replication; MLE-Bench is machine-learning engineering; RE-Bench is AI R&D; DiscoveryBench and SciCode cover data-driven discovery and scientific coding. All provide a fixed task specification. None asks whether the agent could have constructed the workflow itself, none spans general scientific domains at project level, and none varies guidance within the same research problem—so a high score can mean genuine discovery or faithful procedure-following, and the two are indistinguishable in the aggregate.

item.title: Embodied-Navigator: Point, Think, Memorize, and Align for Efficient Navigation
item.description: By Hongyan Feng, Sunlai Chen, Xuanyu Liu (Zhejiang University; Zhejiang Humanoid Robot Innovation Center) Embodied-Navigator: Point, Think, Memorize, and Align for Efficient Navigation. First authors Hongyan Feng, Sunlai Chen, and Xuanyu Liu, from the OmniAl Group of the ACES Lab at Zhejiang University together with the Zhejiang Humanoid Robot Innovation Center. The system is called TAMP-Nav: Point, Think, Memorize, Align. It reports 66.2 percent success on R2R-CE validation-unseen with a tenth of the training trajectories of some competitors, and it runs inference in about half the time per task. Those efficiency numbers are the real story here. Three bottlenecks motivate the design. First, the geometric gap: vision-language models are pretrained on 2D image-text pairs, but vision-and-language navigation forces them to emit low-level atomic actions like turn left thirty degrees or to regress 3D coordinates, which demands implicit geometric transformations they were never trained to perform and produces spatial hallucinations with poor sample efficiency. Second, the reasoning-efficiency dilemma: chain-of-thought improves high-level planning but existing models trigger it at every step or at fixed intervals, multiplying inference latency for marginal gains. Third, memory: keeping full visual history causes attention dilution and overflow, while discarding history or decaying it loses critical information, and most architectures carry no explicit spatio-temporal coordinates organizing what they keep.

item.title: AVA-Encoder: Towards Agent-Native Video Representation Learning
item.description: By Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, Haozhe Wang (Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba; ShanghaiTech University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) AVA-Encoder: Towards Agent-Native Video Representation Learning. First authors Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, and Haozhe Wang, from the Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba, ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Institute of Computing Technology, and Southeast University. The problem: video creation agents cannot learn filmmaking from finished films, because a rendered video is not an operable record of the decisions that produced it—scripts, characters, shots, camera language, pacing, and audio design are coupled across space and time in ways the finished pixels do not expose. The proposal is to turn films into structured knowledge graphs that agents can read, query, edit, and reconstruct from—and to use reconstruction error itself as the training signal. The task formulation is an agentic auto-encoder. Three parts. An Agentic Video Encoder governed by a policy implemented as three distinct system prompts covering film-level, shot-level, and keyframe-level understanding, with inter-level context injection propagating information across granularities. A bottleneck that is not a neural embedding but a Film Knowledge Graph. And a fixed decoder: a static rendering pipeline calling frozen generation models as tools, taking reference keyframes and shot-prompt descriptions from the graph and rendering shots sequentially. Because the decoder never changes, any difference in reconstruction quality measures the representation. That is the entire evaluation philosophy—reconstruction fidelity as a proxy for representation faithfulness.

item.title: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
item.description: By Ziheng Qin, Yaxin Lu, Zhangyang Atlas Wang (Somewhere on the Earth) StateM: Reaching 95.3 percent raw accuracy, or a $15 frontier run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via harness scaling. That is arXiv 2608.15089, from Ziheng Qin, Yaxin Lu, and Zhangyang Atlas Wang, joined by Kai Wang, who list their affiliation on the paper's first page as, literally, "Somewhere on the Earth." The work was done in the authors' personal time. The claim deserves attention anyway: without changing a single model weight, their agent runtime lifts GPT-5.5 xhigh from an 83.1 percent reference to 92.1 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and reaches 95.3 percent raw accuracy with GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh across 445 public-submission trials. Let me walk through what the system actually does, what the evidence does and does not cover, and where you should verify before adopting any of it. The premise is familiar to anyone who has babysat a long agent run: the underlying model clearly knows how to do each step, and the run still fails. The agent drifts off-plan, loses track of mutable task state, skips a required check, repeats an unproductive action, or stops before the deliverable is verifiably complete. Benchmarks score the completed job, not the fraction of steps the model understood. The paper frames the dominant alternative responses — more pretraining, more post-training data, longer reasoning, more agents — as orthogonal to its question: how much apparent model failure is actually failure of the surrounding harness, the layer that maintains state, constrains execution, verifies progress, and recovers from errors? They call systematically improving that layer harness scaling. item.title: Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization
item.description: By Yixuan Wang, Yifei Chen, Haichao Zhang (University of Florida; UC San Diego; Northeastern University; Northwestern University; Stanford University; Zillion Network; Universität Innsbruck) The paper is called Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization. The first three authors are Yixuan Wang, Yifei Chen, and Haichao Zhang, working with a nine-person roster that spans the University of Florida, UC San Diego, Northeastern University, Northwestern University, Stanford University together with Zillion Network, and the University of Innsbruck. The arXiv id is 2608.16072, dated August 18, 2026. Here is the problem they take on, and it is one of those problems that is obvious once stated. Group-relative policy optimization is now the de facto standard for post-training language model reasoners. You sample a group of rollouts per prompt, score them, subtract the group mean, divide by the group standard deviation, and push probabilities accordingly. It works because the baseline comes free from the group. The friction starts when you optimize several reward objectives at once — answer correctness, format compliance, a length penalty, a tool-use check, whatever your mixture happens to be. The universal practice is scalarization: sum the components into one reward, then run the usual group normalization on the total. That sum is where signal leaks out. Consider an objective the model has essentially mastered: every rollout in the group earns nearly the same score on it. Its within-group z-score is then pure sampling noise — tiny, directionless, occasionally nonzero for no reason at all. After scalarization, that noise still participates in the total advantage. It competes with, and dilutes, the genuine signal coming from objectives the model has not mastered yet. The gradient budget gets spent maintaining

item.title: HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds
item.description: By Weiliang Chen, Haowen Sun, Jun Gao, et al. (MirroS Lab) Here is a question the world-model community has mostly been avoiding: how do you trust a score that comes with no explanation? Today's paper is HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds — first authors Weiliang Chen, Haowen Sun, and Jun Gao, joined by co-authors including Jialong Wu, Jiangran Lyu, and Fangfu Liu in a forty-four-author collaboration whose benchmark and tooling ship publicly under the MirroS Lab organization. Their diagnosis is blunt. Current world-model evaluation compresses every prediction into metrics computed brute-force — pixel distances and classifier scores with no reasoning chain anyone can inspect. When two video-world models disagree about whether a cup stays on the table after a robot arm sweeps past, you receive two numbers and zero arguments. This paper's bet is that the evaluator itself should be an agent: something that investigates a generated rollout the way a careful reviewer investigates a manuscript, and leaves behind an evidence trail you can audit line by line. World models are becoming the planning core of embodied systems. An agent imagines forward — if I grasp here, the scene evolves there — and acts on the imagination. As these generators improve, the bottleneck moves from making predictions to grading them, and grading is where the field quietly cut corners. The standard toolkit measures observation overlap frame by frame, plus learned classifiers for physics plausibility. Those scores hide three distinct failure modes inside one average: did the model see what changed, did it predict the right dynamics, and did it remember the object three seconds later? A single blended number answers none of those questions, and because nothing intermediate is written down, you cannot tell a lucky score from an earned one. Worse, leaderboard gaps between rival mod

item.title: ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness
item.description: By Huatong Song, Fei Bai, Ming Yang, et al. (Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China; IQuest Research) Today we're looking at ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness, by Huatong Song, Fei Bai, and Ming Yang, with seventeen more colleagues spread across the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence at Renmin University of China and a lab called IQuest Research. Here's the uncomfortable premise. The agents everyone actually deploys are not naked language models. They're models wrapped in a harness: a planning loop, tool invocations, memory reads and writes, retry logic, maybe a sub-agent or two. And yet almost all reinforcement learning for agents is done on the naked model, on synthetic traces, with the harness treated as something that happens later, at deployment, to someone else. This paper declines that arrangement. It trains the full stack, model plus harness, as one unit, using reinforcement learning that never opens either of them up. The harness stays a black box. The model stays a black box. All the learning signal comes from the outside: did the finished trajectory complete the task, yes or no. That refusal raises the obvious question, which is also why the paper exists: how do you make reinforcement learning work at all when your policy is a sprawling scaffold that takes hundreds of steps per episode? Three reasons, and the paper is upfront about all of them. First, episodes are enormous. A single rollout through a real harness on a real task can run for hundreds of turns, and because the whole running conversation ships back to the model on every one of them, total token spend grows much faster than the episode does. Second, the environments are live software: browsers, terminals, office suites. They are slow, stateful, and they break. Third, there are no gradients. item.title: How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks
item.description: By Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, Xinmiao Yu, et al. (Prentis AI, Stanford University, Titan Holdings) Welcome back to the show. What actually breaks when you hand a hundred real research problems to a frontier coding agent and let it run unsupervised? We finally have a careful answer, and it isn't flattered. The paper is "How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks," by Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, and Xinmiao Yu, with colleagues at Prentis AI, Stanford University, and Titan Holdings. The number that defines it: in 82.5 percent of audited runs, the agent diagnosed its own critical flaw during self-review, wrote that diagnosis down, and then reported the unrevised conclusion anyway. Found it, documented it, shipped it. The benchmark behind that statistic is AutoResearchEval — one hundred tasks from real frontier scientific work across seven domains, each specified through seven fields: the query states the job while the grading target stays withheld. Seventy tasks are open-ended — a premise plus an unresolved tension, scored on process, not outcome — and thirty carry a measurable anchor. The team ran eight harness–model combinations: Claude Code carrying six backbones, plus Codex CLI and Gemini CLI with one each. That yielded 800 full trajectories, roughly seventy-three thousand tool calls, averaging ninety-two steps per run. Scoring those runs is the second contribution. Instead of one language-model call reading a transcript, an artifact-aware agent-as-a-judge receives the complete evidence package — code, execution logs, final report, data files. Its rubric demands dedicated sections per lifecycle stage, evidence anchors like log lines or exact values, and nine iron rules distilled from earlier rounds. item.title: Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation
item.description: By Yijiang Li, Yijun Liang, Yunjie Tian (UC San Diego; University of Maryland, College Park; Georgia Institute of Technology; Johns Hopkins University; University of Oxford) Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation, by Yijiang Li of UC San Diego, Yijun Liang of the University of Maryland, College Park, and Yunjie Tian, an independent researcher, with co-authors from Georgia Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins University, and the University of Oxford. On-policy distillation works because the teacher knows something the student does not: either it is a bigger model, or someone hands it privileged material such as reference answers or ground-truth regions of interest. This paper asks where the asymmetry comes from when you have none of that, and the answer is refreshingly blunt: take information away from the student instead of giving it to the teacher. Train the student on degraded views of the image while an exponential-moving-average copy of itself scores the same prefixes under the clean image. No annotations, no rewards, no second model. Whether that trick survives contact with real benchmarks is the question, so let us look at the numbers rather than the framing. The method, called S2VOPD, is deliberately thin. For each image-question pair, the student samples its own rollouts conditioned on a transformed view, x-tilde equals T of x, while an EMA teacher re-evaluates every visited prefix using the original clean image. The training objective minimizes a per-token divergence between the teacher distribution given the clean view and the student distribution given the corrupted view, averaged along trajectories the student generated itself, which keeps supervision on exactly the prefixes the student visits at inference time. item.title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
item.description: By Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, Hexiang Tan (Meituan; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development, by Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, and Hexiang Tan, from Meituan and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. The premise is that the field evaluates research agents the wrong way. Agents run long closed-loop cycles of proposing changes, executing experiments, reading verifier feedback, and revising, but benchmarks score them on one final number, which hides where progress was gained, where it leaked away, whether accumulated experience helps or hurts later decisions, and whether the harness rather than the model is doing the work. This report decomposes the loop into rule-based process metrics, runs controlled experience-ablation experiments, varies the agent harness, and then asks an LLM judge with human review whether any solution is actually novel. Seven frontier models, thirty-six tasks, three rollouts each, roughly one hundred thousand U.S. dollars in inference spend. That budget buys credibility; read on for what it bought. The setup first. Tasks come from AutoLab in four families: Model Development with seven tasks, System Optimization with fifteen, Puzzle and Challenge with ten, and CUDA with four. Each task ships a correct but deliberately suboptimal starting artifact, an expert reference solution, a wall-clock budget between two and twelve hours, and an automated verifier scoring zero to one against that scale. Seven models were evaluated: Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.7-Code, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and LongCat-2.0. The main comparison holds Claude Code version 2.1.152 fixed as a shared harness across all models; native harnesses and OpenCode enter only in a dedicated ablation. item.title: SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning
item.description: By Haonan He, Haodi Lei, Yun Luo (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory) SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning, by Haonan He, Haodi Lei, and Yun Luo, with the SU-01 Team at Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. The problem is specific and practical. On-policy distillation is now a standard post-training tool: the student generates its own trajectories, and a teacher provides dense token-level supervision on exactly the states the student visits. But nearly all published work assumes teacher and student share a vocabulary. Try distilling from a long-context reasoning teacher that writes hundred-thousand-token proofs into a short-context student from a different model family, and three things break: the tokenizers do not align, the teacher prefers responses longer than the student's context budget, and training destabilizes into length explosion, truncation, and repetition loops. This paper reports what actually breaks when you attempt this transfer and two small fixes that make it work. The results are strong enough to matter; the mechanism is simple enough to ship. The cross-tokenizer alignment first, because it is the load-bearing idea. Rather than mapping one vocabulary onto another, SimpleOPD performs distillation in shared text space. The student generates a response under its own tokenizer and chat template. That response string is appended to the context reconstructed under the teacher's own chat template, and the teacher tokenizes it natively. Then a linear two-pointer scan walks both tokenizations of the identical response string: whenever the accumulated text prefixes match and the current tokens contribute the exact same text span, the pair is aligned and inherits supervision; partially overlapping spans are skipped entirely, because you cannot uniquely assign one teacher log-probability across mu

item.title: Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning
item.description: By Kai Chen, Jifeng Ding, Ning Ding (Shanghai AI Laboratory) Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning, by Kai Chen, Jifeng Ding, and Ning Ding, with the Intern-S2-Mobius Team at the Shanghai AI Laboratory. The claim is architectural and blunt: binding knowledge storage, the feed-forward network, to reasoning operators, self-attention, layer by layer inside every Transformer block wastes both compute and parameters. Mobius-v0 cuts that binding. One globally shared Memory, built from feed-forward parameters, stores knowledge vectors; multiple Reasoner layers, built from self-attention, iteratively query it through their hidden states. Every reasoning layer reads the entire knowledge repository rather than only what the previous layer passed down. The paper reports a seven-billion-parameter model trained from scratch matching a Transformer baseline's downstream score using sixty-two point six percent of the training data, and a thirty-five-billion production model converted from Qwen3.5 delivering nearly four times end-to-end inference speedup at comparable quality. Those are strong claims for an architecture paper, so the details deserve scrutiny. Two design choices do the work. First, backward residual connection. Standard residuals are unidirectional: shallow states can be read by deep layers, but deep-layer attention processes only knowledge originating from shallow layers. If critical knowledge fails to activate early, the model compensates by generating low-information tokens in an explicit chain of thought and trying again next forward pass. A direct bidirectional residual is infrastructure-hostile, so Mobius gets the effect indirectly: since all Reasoners share one memory, every layer accesses everything, which functions as a backward path. item.title: MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences
item.description: By Xinle Deng, Yida Xue, Xiangyuan Ru (OPPO; OpenKG) MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences, by Xinle Deng, Yida Xue, and Xiangyuan Ru, from OPPO and the OpenKG community. The argument is that agent memory research has been solving the wrong problem in the wrong place. Cloud memory benchmarks assume infinite storage, centralized databases, and conversation-shaped data. Real deployment for next-generation assistants happens on phones, glasses, wearables, and cars, where memory must be multimodal, cross-app, temporally continuous, and built under hard storage, power, latency, and privacy constraints, with raw data never leaving the device. MobileMem is both a benchmark and a framework for on-device long-term memory grounded in roughly one year-scale collection of mobile experiences, and its evaluation results are unflattering to essentially every current memory system. If you build personal assistants, this is a requirements document disguised as a paper. The architecture vision first, because it shapes the benchmark design. Rather than screenshot-scraping everything the user does, the authors observe that modern apps already function as specialized memory systems: browsers keep timestamped searchable histories, finance apps aggregate transactions into monthly summaries, notes apps store structured records. They formalize a two-layer composite ecosystem. A system-level memory layer attached to the assistant acts as a blackboard holding global user state, cross-app preferences, and behavioral abstractions. Application-specific memories act as knowledge sources doing cognitive offloading, filtering transient interface noise like scrolls and page switches and forwarding only meaningful events through a standardized protocol with explicit permission control. item.title: Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation
item.description: By Guibin Zhang, Jiayang Lyu, Ran Sun (National University of Singapore; Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications; Shanghai Jiao Tong University) Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation, by Guibin Zhang of the National University of Singapore, Jiayang Lyu of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, and Ran Sun, with co-authors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The paper addresses the central design question in self-evolving agents: when a model teaches itself from experience, what should the teacher be allowed to see? On-policy self-distillation answers this today with designer-specified artifacts. The teacher gets verified reasoning traces, or final answers, or environment feedback, or successful sibling rollouts, or retrieved documents, and each variant works somewhere and fails somewhere else. LOPD's move is structural rather than incremental: stop hand-designing the privilege entirely. Compose retrieved raw trajectories into continuous latent tokens, make that composition learnable end-to-end alongside the student, and let gradient descent decide what experience is worth encoding for supervision. After training you throw away everything except the student. The mechanics, concretely. An experience bank stores successful rollouts offline as task descriptions plus compact action-result traces with verbose observations stripped. At training time a dense retriever fetches entries by cosine similarity over task-trace pairs, defaulting to three. A composer then processes each retrieved item: an encoder with trainable LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone maps the task-experience pair into hidden states, and a QFormer-style cross-attention compressor with learned queries squeezes variable-length states into exactly thirty-two continuous latent tokens per experience, ninety-six tokens total. item.title: DarwinX: Evolving Agent Harnesses Through Natural Selection
item.description: By Yifan Zhang, Yutong Dai, Juntao Tan (Salesforce AI Research; Salesforce Agentforce) DarwinX: Evolving Agent Harnesses Through Natural Selection, by Yifan Zhang, Yutong Dai, Juntao Tan, and colleagues at Salesforce AI Research and Salesforce Agentforce. The premise: an agent's capability lives partly in its harness, the prompts, tools, skills, memory, and control flow wrapped around the model, and that harness can be improved by selection over a population rather than by editing a single lineage. The underlying model, Salesforce's proprietary Monet agent, stays frozen in every experiment, so every reported delta is attributable to the harness alone. Fitness comes exclusively from each benchmark's own verifier: no gold solutions, no hand-picked winners. The motivation comes from two documented failure modes in self-improving agents. First, path dependence: single-lineage self-editors such as SICA plateau because early edits bias everything downstream. Second, cross-task interference: an edit that fixes one family of tasks silently regresses another, which stalls evolution over mixed task distributions. The Darwin Godel Machine, the closest prior system, mutates one parent at a time and scores the child against that parent, so lineages that solve complementary tasks are never brought back together, and a gain carries no obligation to hold what it displaces. HarnessX isolates task families to contain interference but leaves the resulting specialists in separate lineages. DarwinX keeps the common inner loop, batch rollouts, reflect, propose a bounded edit, gate on regression, and changes the selection wrapped around it.

item.title: DreamX-Phi 1.0: Action-Conditioned Video World Model for Robotic Manipulation
item.description: By DreamX Team, Rui Chen, Xiangxiang Chu (AMAP-ML) DreamX-Phi 1.0: Action-Conditioned Video World Model for Robotic Manipulation, by the DreamX Team, Rui Chen, Xiangxiang Chu, and colleagues at AMAP-ML. This is an action-conditioned video world model for bimanual robotic manipulation: given one observed RGB frame, a language instruction, and a prescribed action sequence of end-effector poses and gripper states, it predicts the resulting future video. The report matters for a specific reason: photorealistic prediction is not the same as faithful prediction. A rollout can look convincing while moving the wrong arm or losing the manipulated object entirely, and this paper is organized almost entirely around closing that gap between visual plausibility and physical correctness. At submission time the model ranked first on Track 1 and tied for second on Track 2 of the WorldArena 2.0 Challenge, an IROS-affiliated competition, and the authors commit to releasing model weights and inference code after the challenge concludes. The base architecture is Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, a five-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer trained under a flow-matching objective; the first frame's VAE latent provides visual context and future-frame latents are learned from there. The interesting engineering is in how actions enter the network. Common practice compresses trajectories into low-dimensional tokens or additive modulation, which leaves rigid-body structure implicit. DreamX-Phi instead reuses PRoPE, projective relative positional encoding, which was originally designed so camera geometry modulates attention. Here each arm's end-effector frame at each latent timestep is expressed relative to arm one's initial pose, translations are normalized by a single motion-amplitude factor computed as the largest displacement over all arms and frames, so resting arm separation does not dominate scale

item.title: How Can Rhetoric Reward-Hack AI Reviewers? Dissecting Rhetorical Sensitivity in AI-Based Peer Review
item.description: By Ming Li, Chenguang Wang, Xirui Li (University of Maryland; Virginia Tech; MBZUAI; University of Waterloo) How Can Rhetoric Reward-Hack AI Reviewers? Dissecting Rhetorical Sensitivity in AI-Based Peer Review, by Ming Li, Chenguang Wang, Xirui Li, Xinyue Zeng, and colleagues at the University of Maryland, Virginia Tech, MBZUAI, and the University of Waterloo. The question is precise: when the reported science is held fixed and only the rhetoric moves, which rhetorical dimensions shift AI reviewer scores, in which direction, and under what conditions. This matters to anyone wiring LLMs into review pipelines, because authors already use LLMs to revise manuscripts and venues are experimenting with LLM reviewers, and the two uses meet in one pipeline. Prior work showed presentation-only edits can raise AI review scores; this paper maps the structure of that vulnerability instead of just demonstrating it exists. The experimental machine is substantial. From OpenReview, the authors sampled 120 anonymized ICLR 2026 submissions, twenty from each of six human-rating bands spanning one to eight point five, matched them to public arXiv LaTeX sources using token-based cosine similarity and five-gram Jaccard similarity to pick the right version, ran an agentic anonymization pass removing author names, affiliations, acknowledgments, status statements, and identity-bearing links with manual verification of both source and compiled PDF, and treated each verified project as a common baseline. item.title: Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus
item.description: By Zunhai Su, Bohan Sun, Xialie Zhuang (Startlux; Tsinghua University; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences; The University of Hong Kong; University of Sydney; Columbia University) Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus, by Zunhai Su, Bohan Sun, Xialie Zhuang, Shuibai Zhang, and colleagues at Startlux, Tsinghua University, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, The University of Hong Kong, the University of Sydney, and Columbia University. If you ship hybrid architectures, models interleaving cheap linear attention layers with occasional full attention layers, this is the first systematic map of what massive activations do inside them. Massive activations are the sparse hidden-state entries that exceed typical activation values by orders of magnitude and concentrate on specific tokens; in full attention transformers they are tightly coupled to attention sinks and have been implicated in attention dynamics generally. The question here is what layerwise interleaving does to them, and the answer turns out to be structured enough to matter for anyone debugging or quantizing these models. The setup first. A hybrid linear attention model alternates sequence-mixing layers: full softmax attention, which is content-dependent but quadratic in sequence length, and linear attention variants that keep a fixed-size recurrent state and run in linear time. The hybridization ratio rho counts sequence-mixing layers per full attention layer; twelve to one means one full attention layer per twelve mixing layers, and one to one recovers a plain transformer. item.title: PlayWorld: Benchmarking World Models with Agent Players over Long-Horizon Objectives
item.description: By Kaixin Ding, Xi Chen, Minghong Cai (The University of Hong Kong; Kling Team at Kuaishou Technology; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Zhejiang University) PlayWorld: Benchmarking World Models with Agent Players over Long-Horizon Objectives, by Kaixin Ding, Xi Chen, Minghong Cai, and colleagues at The University of Hong Kong, the Kling Team at Kuaishou Technology, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, and Zhejiang University. The paper attacks a real methodological gap in how interactive video world models get evaluated. Fixed action trajectories, the standard protocol, are a poor cross-model instrument because action granularity differs per model: the same three camera commands may complete a full 360-degree rotation in one system and only a partial turn in another, so whether a landmark leaves and re-enters view is an artifact of the controller, not a property of the world model. A human player instead pursues long-horizon objectives, turning fully around to check environmental consistency or walking into water to see if ripples form. PlayWorld operationalizes that judgment with an automated agent, producing what is currently the most complete like-for-like comparison of nine state-of-the-art world models. The mechanism has three parts. First, an Agent Player: a replaceable multimodal model, Claude Haiku in the headline runs, wrapped in an interface that translates abstract controls into each world model's native input format over continuous W, A, S, D, arrow-key, and WAIT commands, including browser automation for web-only closed models like Genie 3. item.title: AutoDesign: Meta-Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Design
item.description: By Yaxin Luo, Haobin Jiang, Jialv Zou (Meituan; MBZUAI; Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Peking University; Tsinghua University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shanghai Jiao Tong University) AutoDesign: Meta-Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Design, by Yaxin Luo, Haobin Jiang, Jialv Zou, and colleagues, a fourteen-author collaboration spanning Meituan, MBZUAI, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Peking University, Tsinghua University, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The paper's premise is that the harness around a language model, the prompts, tools, runtime, and evaluation loop that turn a source document into a finished artifact, should be an optimization target in its own right, distinct from model weights. Rather than hand-tuning that scaffold, AutoDesign runs a meta-level optimizer: a coding agent recursively rewrites the design harness itself based on rollout feedback, under an acceptance gate that blocks regressions. The team instantiates this on academic paper-to-poster generation and ships two artifacts worth your attention: DesignHarness, the evolved poster-generation system, and PosterBench, a frozen hundred-paper evaluation protocol with controlled tracks. The formulation is clean. A design harness H is the system surrounding a fixed model that maps a multimodal source x and context c to a human-facing artifact y through an execution trajectory. The objective is the expected quality of produced artifacts under an evaluator R meta, and the meta-harness searches for the harness that maximizes it while model parameters stay fixed throughout. item.title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill
item.description: By Zhuoyang Qian, Biao Wu, Yiran Wang (Vast Intelligence Lab; University of Technology Sydney) Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill, by Zhuoyang Qian, Biao Wu, and Yiran Wang, from the Vast Intelligence Lab and the University of Technology Sydney. The premise: an entire research pipeline, literature retrieval through experiments, figures, and a compiled manuscript, implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an ordinary coding assistant, with no orchestration server, no graph database, and no separate agent platform. For teams already living inside tools like Claude Code, that deployment story matters more than any benchmark delta, so let us take the system apart. The gap the authors claim is real enough. Standalone autonomous-research systems such as AI Scientist, AI Scientist-v2, Agent Laboratory, and Kosmos match or exceed the pipeline breadth but ship as dedicated codebases with their own infrastructure, sometimes a graph database or cluster scheduler on top. Lightweight skill-based writing assistants stay inside the coding assistant but neither run real experiments end to end nor produce editable vector figures rather than embedded bitmaps, the two capabilities at the center of this paper. The closest prior analogue pairs an automated researcher with an automated reviewer trained to critique it, but still stops short of executing experiments. Spark-to-Paper positions itself between those poles, and to its credit the paper marks its own comparison table and breadth chart as ordinal assessments derived from each compared system's public documentation rather than measurements. Keep that caveat in mind whenever the positioning figure comes up.

item.title: OpenART: Scaling Agent Red Teaming via Open-Ended Environment Evolution
item.description: By Yunhao Chen, Xin Wang, Yixu Wang (Fudan University; Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; XSafeAI) OpenART: Scaling Agent Red Teaming via Open-Ended Environment Evolution, by Yunhao Chen, Xin Wang, and Yixu Wang, from Fudan University, the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, and XSafeAI. The core reframing: stop treating a prompt as the unit of red teaming and treat the persistent executable environment as the unit instead. The task objective and safety contract stay fixed while only the target-visible state evolves across rounds. If you ship coding agents against real workspaces, the headline finding should get your attention: pooled strict attack success of 85 percent across 75 agent-model configurations, with environment evolution gaining almost nothing on simple tasks but up to 17.6 points on the most complex ones. First, scale, because that is what separates this from prior agent-safety benchmarks. Over 10,000 validated stateful scenarios spanning 50 domains organized into eight groups, from software and IT data with 13 domains down to digital work and knowledge with 3, grounded in real capability surfaces such as Jira, Slack, GitHub, Gmail, Salesforce, Notion, Figma, Grafana, and dbt. The scenario corpus draws on more than 500,000 tools, MCPs, and skills collected following SkillNet. Median workload is 97 tool calls per scenario with an interquartile range of 90 to 100, dependency depth 32, parallel width 12.5, 96.5 state objects, and 7.5 persistent file formats per task, against 1 to 15 tool calls for InjeAgent, AgentDojo, AgentHarm, ASB, ToolEmu, and DTap, none of which persist state across file formats at all. item.description: By Cheng Qian, Wenting Zhao, Liangwei Yang (Salesforce AI Research; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses, by Cheng Qian, Wenting Zhao, and Liangwei Yang, from Salesforce AI Research and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The question is clean: can a strong builder model write inference-time scaffolding that lifts a weak target model without touching a single parameter? The answer across 72 controlled runs is yes, dramatically. GPT-5.4-mini's macro accuracy on four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks goes from 0.488 to a best of 0.912, and the mechanism analysis tells you exactly where the gains come from, which is what makes this paper useful rather than just another leaderboard entry. Setup first, because the protocol is what makes the result credible. Four benchmarks aggregate into a hidden test set of 3,900 items: BigToM with 1,200 binary belief, goal, and action questions hinging on whether an agent observed a world change, procedurally generated from causal templates; Hi-ToM with 1,200 nested belief questions across recursion orders zero through four with deception and multi-room object tracking; MMToM-QA with 600 binary Bayesian goal and belief inference items from action traces in household settings; MuMA-ToM with 900 three-choice questions over goals, beliefs, and beliefs about others' goals in embodied multi-agent interactions. Only text-format questions are used. Each builder gets only a 195-item validation slice, 5 percent drawn by fixed seed, plus a rule file describing task instructions and submission format and a demonstration file showing how to call the target. item.description: By Mengru Wang, Junfeng Fang, Shuofei Qiao (Zhejiang University; National University of Singapore; Southern University of Science and Technology) Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence, by Mengru Wang, Junfeng Fang, and Shuofei Qiao, from Zhejiang University, the National University of Singapore, the Southern University of Science and Technology, Heriot-Watt University, UC San Diego, and Northeastern University. Three case results anchor it: a cross-modal subliminal learning risk, a causal theory of belief-state heads, and mechanism-guided steering of a DNA foundation model. The infrastructure is the first real contribution. An interpretability-focused knowledge graph of roughly 13,000 papers plus research blogs, built on an OpenAlex-derived corpus, organized along three axes: object of study, application scenario, and analysis method. In its current form it holds about 13,900 interpretability papers, over 107,000 nodes, and roughly 1.86 million edges. DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking extracted attributes with unsupported or ambiguous items deliberately left unspecified rather than inferred. Quality control used Claude Opus 4.7 as an LLM judge plus three human annotators auditing 100 sampled records, yielding accuracy above 90 percent, with disagreements feeding back into extraction prompts before reprocessing. This graph plugs into SciAtlas, a multidisciplinary database of more than 43 million papers across 26 fields. item.title: SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries
item.description: By Xingyu Tan, Xiaoyang Wang, Qing Liu (UNSW Sydney; CSIRO) SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries, by Xingyu Tan, Xiaoyang Wang, and Qing Liu, from UNSW Sydney and CSIRO. The problem will be familiar to anyone running a skill library at scale: skills are retrieved as whole packages, compressed as plain text, and turned into execution graphs only after retrieval, and that unit mismatch is exactly where things fail. Whole-skill exposure wastes context on irrelevant sections, text summarization can silently drop a precondition or a verifier hook, and task-time graph compilation never improves the library itself. SkillZip's answer is to make the section-level procedural graph the persistent storage format, then compress it in a way that provably keeps procedures executable. The representation comes first. Each skill package is decomposed by Sec2Graph into typed section nodes with nine execution roles: Intent, Trigger, Input, Precondition, Operation, Resource, Failure, Verifier, Output. Segmentation uses headings, lists, code blocks, warnings, argument descriptions, tool references, and tests as boundary cues, with a model-assisted parser refining when cues run out, always preserving source pointers back to the original text; role assignment is semantic, so in a tabular skill infer-the-delimiter is an Operation while verify-row-counts-unchanged is a Verifier regardless of file position. Each node carries input-output signatures, resources, guard and verifier conditions, and provenance. Edges come in four kinds: typed dependencies such as requires, binds, uses-resource, verifies, and repairs; weak-order edges for local sequence inside a skill; skill-membership edges; and equivalence links connecting compatible occurrences to shared canonical prototypes that expose cross-skill reuse, like tabular ingestion shared by cleaning, pivo

If that sounds soft, note the authors' own framing applies directly to coding agents, where a new request must not silently break implemented behavior, interface contracts, tests, or safety requirements. Human experts clean the candidate pool of duplicate records, mismatched characters, and incomplete synopses, then manually select 100 movies to maximize genre spread across 18 categories, action and science fiction leading at 13 and 12 percent, comedy 11, western 9, fantasy 8, crime 7.
